item.title: Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) IPO Process: A Practical Research Report
item.description:
Listing eligibility, review procedures, key deadlines and practical considerations for the Main Board and GEM.

Information current as of 26 November 2026. The rule basis is the Main Board Listing Rules and GEM Listing Rules currently in force, together with public documents of HKEX and the SFC.

1. Executive Summary

This report sets out the complete initial public offering (IPO) process on the Main Board and GEM of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX), focusing on three questions: who can list, who does the work, and in what sequence and over what timeframe. All rule references are drawn from the Main Board Listing Rules and GEM Listing Rules currently in force and from public documents of HKEX and the SFC, with a clause index and sources listed in the appendices.

1.1 Five Key Conclusions

① Dual-track regulation. The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK, an HKEX subsidiary) reviews listing eligibility and rule compliance; the SFC concurrently reviews disclosure through “dual filing” and may object to an application or impose conditions; the prospectus must also be registered under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32).

② Four hard deadlines. An A1 may be filed only after the sponsor has been formally appointed for a full 2 months; an A1 remains valid for 6 months; the prospectus must be substantially finalised 4 “full business days” before the hearing; a returned application may be resubmitted only after 8 weeks.

③ Three financial tests on the Main Board. Profit test; market capitalisation/revenue/cash flow test; market capitalisation/revenue test. Pre-revenue biotech and Specialist Technology companies may follow Chapter 18A and Chapter 18C respectively.

④ Typical timeline. About 8–15 months from formal sponsor appointment to listing, and about 6–12 months from A1 submission. These are market experience figures; the rules themselves set only caps and checkpoints, not committed timelines.

⑤ Recent changes. From August 2025 public float follows a new market-cap-tiered scale; FINI has compressed IPO settlement to T+2; the market-wide T+1 target is the second half of 2028.

1.2 Scope and Methodology

  • Basis: HKEX’s electronic Main Board Listing Rules (including Chapters 3A, 8, 9, 11A, 12, 18A and 18C), Chapter 11 of the GEM Listing Rules, the Main Board Fees Rules, Practice Notes PN18/PN22, the SFC dual filing page and HKEX market information pages.
  • Conventions: unless otherwise stated, all amounts are in Hong Kong dollars; “typical duration” and “usual practice” reflect market experience and are not rule commitments; rule provisions are governed by the English text, and the Chinese wording is a paraphrase for readability.
  • As at: information is current as of 26 November 2026. Rules are amended frequently, and live transactions should rely on the version in force at the time of submission.

2. The Hong Kong IPO Market and Listing Architecture

2.1 Market Position

Hong Kong is one of the world’s leading equity fundraising markets. According to HKEX, Hong Kong ranked first globally by IPO proceeds in 2025, raising more than US$36 billion over the year; since the new economy listing regime was introduced in 2018, more than 430 new economy companies have listed in Hong Kong, raising over US$150 billion in aggregate. As at 2025, around 167 biotech companies had listed under Chapter 18A.

The direct implication for issuers is that the Hong Kong market provides two sources of capital—international institutional money and Mainland Chinese money (through the mutual access mechanisms)—and has dedicated channels for weighted voting rights, pre-revenue biotech, Specialist Technology, SPACs and other special structures, giving issuers considerable choice of board.

2.2 Listing Architecture and Boards

Table 1 HKEX Listing Boards and Special Channels

Board / Chapter Positioning Core features
Main Board For mature companies with a certain scale and profit/revenue track record Three financial tests; higher market cap threshold; weighted voting rights permitted (Chapter 8A)
GEM For small and medium-sized growth companies Two tests with lower thresholds; public float and disclosure requirements converging with the Main Board
Chapter 18A Pre-revenue biotech companies Market cap ≥ HK$1.5 billion; core product, R&D pipeline and sophisticated investor requirements
Chapter 18C Specialist Technology companies (next-generation information technology, advanced hardware, advanced materials, new energy, new food and agriculture technology) Two market cap thresholds for “commercialised” and “pre-commercial” companies; R&D investment requirements
Chapter 18B Special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs) Listing and fundraising first, target acquisition later; special constraints on promoters and dilution caps
Chapter 19C Secondary listing of qualifying overseas issuers Already primarily listed on a qualifying exchange; existing structures may be retained

Source: HKEX Main Board Listing Rules chapter structure and the listing boards introduction page; threshold figures are given in Chapter 3.

2.3 Regulatory Division of Roles

Table 2 Principal Regulators and Service Providers in an IPO

Institution Role in an IPO
The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK, an HKEX subsidiary) Receives and reviews listing applications; the Listing Committee conducts the hearing and makes the listing decision; ongoing post-listing supervision
Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) Operates dual filing under the Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules; reviews disclosure documents; may object to an application or impose conditions
Companies Registry Registers the prospectus under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (registration is required before issue)
Hong Kong Securities Clearing Company (HKSCC) / FINI IPO settlement platform; handles subscriptions, allotment, settlement and share crediting
Department of Justice / other regulators Sector-dependent (e.g. financial services, healthcare, telecommunications, data compliance)

Note: SEHK and the SFC do not approve “in series” but review in parallel and keep each other informed; the process can proceed to hearing and launch only when neither has an objection.

3. Listing Eligibility and Board Selection

3.1 The Three Financial Tests on the Main Board

A Main Board applicant must satisfy one of three tests (Rule 8.05). The “soft” conditions common to all three are a trading record of not less than three financial years, management continuity over the three most recent financial years, and ownership continuity over the most recent audited financial year.

Table 3 The Three Financial Tests on the Main Board (Rule 8.05)

Test Financial criteria Key points
Profit test Profit attributable to shareholders ≥ HK$35 million in the most recent year; ≥ HK$45 million in aggregate for the two preceding years Profit must arise from ordinary business and exclude non-recurring gains and losses; suited to companies with stable earnings
Market cap/revenue/cash flow test Market cap at listing ≥ HK$2 billion; revenue in the most recent audited year ≥ HK$500 million; operating cash flow ≥ HK$100 million in aggregate for the three preceding years Suited to companies with large revenue and robust cash flow whose profit is affected by depreciation or expansion
Market cap/revenue test Market cap at listing ≥ HK$4 billion; revenue in the most recent audited year ≥ HK$500 million Suited to companies with high valuations and high revenue but insufficient current profit (waivers are addressed in Rule 8.05A)

Note: All three tests require a trading record of at least three financial years; Chapter 18A and 18C applicants may be exempt from Rule 8.05 and are assessed under their respective chapters.

3.2 Other Quantitative Conditions on the Main Board

Table 4 Other Quantitative Requirements on the Main Board (Summary)

Item Requirement Provision
Expected market cap Total market cap at listing ≥ HK$500 million 8.09(2)
Market cap of public float Market cap of securities held by the public ≥ HK$125 million 8.09(1)
Market cap per class of securities Market cap of the class to be listed ≥ HK$50 million (HK$10 million for warrants, etc.) 8.09(3)
Public float percentage Market cap ≤ HK$6 billion: 25%; HK$6 billion–HK$30 billion: the higher of the percentage that brings the public float to HK$1.5 billion and 15%; > HK$30 billion: the higher of the percentage that brings the public float to HK$4.5 billion and 10% 8.08(1)
Number of shareholders At least 300 shareholders at listing 8.08(2)
Shareholding concentration The top three public shareholders must not beneficially own more than 50% of the public float 8.08(3)
Free float Shares free from any disposal restrictions ≥ 10% and market cap ≥ HK$50 million, or market cap ≥ HK$600 million Related to Rule 8.08
Sponsor At least one sponsor independent of the applicant; an application may be submitted only after 2 full months of formal appointment 3A.07, 3A.02B

Note: The public float table is the new framework effective 4 August 2025, replacing the previous flat 25% requirement (large-cap issuers were previously allowed flexibility within 15%–25%).

3.3 The Two GEM Tests

Table 5 GEM Listing Eligibility (Rule 11.12A and Rule 11.23)

Test Financial criteria Other
Cash flow test Trading record of not less than two financial years; operating cash flow ≥ HK$30 million in aggregate for the two preceding financial years Market cap ≥ HK$150 million; two years of management continuity
Market cap/revenue/R&D test Market cap ≥ HK$250 million; revenue ≥ HK$100 million in aggregate over the two preceding years and growing year on year; R&D expenditure ≥ HK$30 million in aggregate over the two preceding years, with R&D expenditure at least 15% of total operating expenditure each year For R&D-driven Specialist Technology-type companies
Public float (common to both) Market cap of public float ≥ HK$45 million; at least 100 public shareholders; public float percentage per the same market-cap-tiered table as the Main Board (25%/15%/10%) Rule 11.23

Note: GEM accountant’s reports must cover at least two financial years (three on the Main Board), and the latest financial period must not end more than 6 months before the date of the prospectus.

3.4 Thresholds for the Special Channels

Table 6 Key Thresholds of Chapters 18A/18C

Channel Eligible applicants Key thresholds
Chapter 18A biotech Biotech companies unable to pass the Rule 8.05 financial tests Market cap at listing ≥ HK$1.5 billion; the existing business must have at least one “core product” that has passed the concept stage and is under R&D; investment by at least one sophisticated investor before listing; working capital covering at least 125% of costs for at least 12 months; an R&D and commercialisation plan for the core product
Chapter 18C Specialist Technology Companies principally engaged in the R&D and commercialisation of Specialist Technology products/services Commercialised companies: market cap at listing ≥ HK$6 billion and Specialist Technology revenue ≥ HK$250 million in the most recent audited year; pre-commercial companies: market cap at listing ≥ HK$10 billion; recognition as “Specialist Technology” depends on R&D expenditure as a share of total expenditure and the proportion of R&D personnel

Note: The two Chapter 18C market cap thresholds—“commercialised” and “pre-commercial”—are HK$6 billion and HK$10 billion respectively; the revenue requirement does not apply to pre-commercial companies. Chapter 18B SPACs are subject to separate promoter eligibility and dilution cap requirements, which this table does not cover.

3.5 Choosing a Board and Test Path

  • Stable profits, moderate size: the profit test is the most direct, with review focused on earnings quality and business sustainability.
  • Large revenue but thin profit: assess the market cap/revenue test first; where operating cash flow is sound, the market cap/revenue/cash flow test requires a lower market cap threshold (HK$2 billion versus HK$4 billion).
  • Pre-revenue biotech: Chapter 18A; the R&D progress of core products and sophisticated investors are the focus of review.
  • Specialist Technology (including AI, robotics and new materials): Chapter 18C; first determine whether the company is “commercialised” or “pre-commercial”—there is a HK$4 billion gap between the two market cap thresholds.
  • Small and medium-sized enterprises: GEM has lower thresholds, and of the two tests the cash flow test imposes no hard profit requirement, suiting companies with steady operating cash flow.

4. Participants and Their Responsibilities

Hong Kong IPO intermediaries are highly specialised, with clearly defined and mutually balancing roles. The sponsor is the only party accountable to SEHK for the “overall quality of the application” and is the statutory channel for regulatory communication.

Table 7 Principal Participants

Role Principal responsibilities Qualifications / key points
Sponsor Leads due diligence, organises preparation of the listing document, files Form A1 on behalf of the applicant and liaises with SEHK/SFC, issues the sponsor’s declaration SFC-licensed corporation (Type 6 regulated activity); at least one must be independent; must perform due diligence under PN21; must notify SEHK in writing upon appointment
Overall coordinator (OC) Oversees bookbuilding, price discovery, allocation and price stabilisation; coordinates the underwriting syndicate For new listings involving bookbuilding placings, at least one sponsor (or its group member) must also act as OC, or the applicant must confirm in writing that it has a “sponsor-OC”
Underwriter / bookrunner Underwrites or places securities and builds investor demand Licensed corporation; bears underwriting obligations under the underwriting agreement
Reporting accountant Issues the accountant’s report under Chapter 4 (three years on the Main Board / two years on GEM) and reviews internal controls and financial information Hong Kong practising accountant (HKICPA member firm)
Legal adviser (Hong Kong) Legal sections of the listing document, regulatory compliance, company and securities law opinions Familiar with the Listing Rules and the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance
Legal adviser (PRC/offshore) Domestic compliance (licences, land, labour, tax, data) / Cayman, BVI structures and constitutional documents Works with Hong Kong counsel to deliver legal opinions
Valuer Valuations of properties, mining assets, biological assets, etc. Chapter 5 and related guidance; professionally qualified
Internal control adviser Pre-listing internal control review and remediation recommendations Market practice (not rule-mandated), but often requested during review
Industry consultant Industry overview, market size and competitive landscape (the “Industry Overview” section of the listing document) Independent third party with credibility
Receiving bank / share registrar / HKSCC Collection of subscription monies, share registration, settlement and crediting Licensed bank; registrar must be approved; FINI platform member

Note: The above is the conventional set-up; specific transactions may add or drop roles depending on sector, structure and size.

5. The Full IPO Process: Six Stages

5.1 Overview of the Stages

Table 8 The Six IPO Stages and Key Deliverables

Stage Key actions and deliverables Main basis Typical duration
1. Preparation and restructuring Board and test-path analysis; equity/structure restructuring; clean-up of competing businesses and connected transactions; bringing in Pre-IPO investors; engaging intermediaries; three-year (or two-year) audit and internal control remediation Chapters 8, 4 6–12 months
2. Sponsor appointment and due diligence Signing the sponsor engagement letter and notifying SEHK in writing; sponsor due diligence under PN21; drafting the initial listing document; preparing the A1 package 3A.02, 3A.02B, PN21 ≥ 2 months (statutory)
3. A1 submission and dual filing Filing Form A1, the Application Proof, the initial listing fee and other documents; publishing the Public AP on the same day if elected; dual filing with the SFC through SEHK 9.03, 9.10A, 12.01A, PN22 T0
4. Review and enquiries Multiple rounds of enquiries from SEHK/SFC; full revision of the listing document each round; progress updates every two weeks; final draft filed 4 full business days before the hearing 9.03(2)(3)(4)(5) 4–6 months
5. Listing Committee hearing The Listing Committee reviews the application and decides (approval / conditional approval / deferral / rejection); review may be sought Chapter 2A, Listing Committee procedures Hearing date
6. Post-hearing launch and listing Receipt of the post-hearing letter; publication of the PHIP; finalising and registering the prospectus; roadshow, bookbuilding and pricing; public offer and placing; FINI settlement; listing 12.01B, 11A.01, PN18 2–4 weeks

Note: “Typical duration” is a range based on market experience and is affected by the number of enquiry rounds, the validity period of financial information and the market window; the 6-month validity of the A1 is a hard constraint.

5.2 Stage 1: Preparation and Restructuring

This stage determines whether the project can pass the hearing smoothly, and its workload is often underestimated. The core task is not “writing materials” but turning the company into an entity that the capital markets can understand and the regulators can accept.

  • Determining the board and test path: first run market cap and financial projections, then work backwards to identify the applicable test; where the profit test applies, ensure that profit in the most recent year and the two preceding years all meet the thresholds, excluding one-off gains.
  • Restructuring: choosing a red-chip / H-share / VIE structure; establishing a Cayman or BVI holding platform; injecting domestic interests; unwinding nominee shareholdings; regularising employee shareholding platforms.
  • Independence and competing business: where a controlling shareholder operates a competing business, the listing document must make full disclosure under Rule 8.10 and demonstrate that the applicant can operate independently; connected transactions must be eliminated or regularised.
  • Pre-IPO investment: the timing, valuation and special rights of investors (repurchase, liquidation preference, etc.) must be properly addressed before submission and are usually required to be terminated or adjusted before listing.
  • Financials and internal controls: preparing three-year (Main Board) or two-year (GEM) statements under the applicable accounting standards (HKFRS/IFRS); revenue recognition, customer concentration and related-party fund flows are frequently queried.
  • Compliance review: licences, environmental protection, work safety, labour and social security, tax, data and cybersecurity, and intellectual property.

5.3 Stage 2: Sponsor Appointment and Due Diligence

The sponsor must be engaged under a written engagement letter and must notify SEHK in writing as soon as practicable after appointment. The key hard rule is that a listing application may not be submitted less than 2 months after the date of the sponsor’s formal appointment; where there are multiple sponsors, the clock runs from the formal appointment of the last sponsor (Rule 3A.02B). In practice this rule makes “finding a sponsor” the starting point of the project timetable.

The sponsor must conduct reasonable due diligence in accordance with Practice Note 21 (PN21) and bears statutory responsibility for material matters in the listing document. In practice the sponsor drives a closed loop of “due diligence checklist—management interviews—third-party verification—working paper archiving” while coordinating lawyers, accountants, valuers and internal control advisers.

5.4 Stage 3: A1 Submission and Dual Filing

The applicant files its listing application on Form A1, completed and signed by the sponsor on its behalf, accompanied by the documents specified in Rule 9.10A(1), the Application Proof (the draft listing document) and the initial listing fee. The rules expressly require the application to be “substantially complete”; otherwise SEHK will return the application, return the documents and deal with fees already paid in accordance with the rules; a returned application may be resubmitted no earlier than 8 weeks after the date of return (Rule 9.03(3)).

There are two points on publication: first, publication of the Application Proof is “optional”—where the applicant elects to publish, it must submit the Public AP for publication on the same day it files its application with SEHK (Rule 12.01A, PN22); second, whether or not the AP is published, the application must be dual-filed with the SFC through SEHK, and the SFC may object to the application or impose conditions under section 6 of the Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules.

The initial listing fee is charged by tier according to the monetary value of the securities to be listed and must be paid in advance at the time of application (see Chapter 7).

5.5 Stage 4: Regulatory Review and Enquiries

Review is conducted concurrently by the SEHK Listing Division and the SFC, typically in the form of multiple rounds of written enquiries (market experience suggests 3–6 rounds, depending on project complexity). The issuer and sponsor must respond round by round and submit a revised listing document. The rules require that revisions not be “fragmented” and that each version fully address all comments on the previous version (Rule 9.03(5)); the applicant must update SEHK on the progress of its application every two weeks (Rule 9.03(2)).

There are two hard timing checkpoints:

  • Six-month validity: if listing is not completed within 6 months from the date of A1 submission, the application lapses and the initial listing fee is not refunded; to continue, a fresh application must be filed and the fee paid again (note 2 to Rule 9.03(1)).
  • Four full business days before the hearing: SEHK may require the hearing to be postponed unless, at least 4 full business days before the hearing, the applicant has submitted a revised listing document containing full disclosure and all outstanding documents, and has satisfactorily resolved the regulatory comments (Rule 9.03(4)).

Review focus is not only whether “the numbers add up” but also whether “the business is real, sustainable and suitable for listing”. Common lines of enquiry are set out in Chapter 9.

5.6 Stage 5: Listing Committee Hearing

The Listing Committee reviews the application at the hearing and decides to approve, give conditional approval, defer consideration or reject. Before the hearing, the sponsor must ensure that the listing document is final, that all waiver applications (if any) have been submitted and that directors and senior management have completed the necessary declarations.

If the application is rejected or approved with conditions, the applicant may apply for a review within the prescribed period, which is considered by the Listing Review Committee. Review is a remedial procedure and should not form part of the normal timetable.

5.7 Stage 6: Post-Hearing Launch and Listing

Once the hearing is passed, the project enters the launch execution phase, with the pace driven by the market window.

  • Publication of the PHIP: after receiving the “post-hearing letter” from SEHK and confirming that the principal comments have been addressed, the applicant must publish the Post Hearing Information Pack on the HKEX website as soon as practicable; this is mandatory (Rule 12.01B, PN22).
  • Finalising and registering the prospectus: the prospectus must comply with the Listing Rules and may be issued only after registration with the Companies Registry under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Rule 11A.01). It may not be issued before SEHK confirms that it has no further comments on the listing document (Rule 9.07).
  • Roadshow and bookbuilding: management roadshow, pre-deal analyst discussions and institutional price discovery; the OC coordinates the order book.
  • Public offer and placing: the public offer portion typically accounts for about 10% of the global offering (subject to upward adjustment on clawback), with the placing accounting for the balance; the public offer is divided by application amount into Pool A (HK$5 million and below) and Pool B (above HK$5 million), with the two pools allocated equally (PN18). Where over-subscription reaches the agreed multiples, clawback applies in accordance with the mechanism disclosed in the prospectus.
  • Pricing, allotment and settlement: allocation is determined after pricing and the allotment results are announced; the FINI platform handles subscription monies and share settlement, and the IPO settlement cycle has been shortened from T+5 to T+2.
  • Listing: trading in the shares begins on SEHK; during the stabilisation period (typically 30 days) the over-allotment option (greenshoe, up to 15%) may be exercised; controlling shareholders must comply with lock-up undertakings.

6. Timetable and Key Deadlines

Table 9 Key Deadlines Set by the Rules

Matter Deadline Basis
Formal sponsor appointment → A1 submission Not less than 2 months Rule 3A.02B
A1 submission → application lapse 6 months (lapses if not completed; fee not refunded) Note 2 to Rule 9.03(1)
Application returned → resubmission Not less than 8 weeks Rule 9.03(3)
Filing of the final draft and outstanding documents before the hearing 4 full business days before the hearing Rule 9.03(4)
Progress updates on the application Every two weeks Rule 9.03(2)
Publication of the Public AP (if elected) Same day as A1 submission PN22 paragraph 9
Publication of the PHIP As soon as practicable after the post-hearing letter Rule 12.01B, PN22
Prospectus registration Completed before issue Rule 11A.01
Period covered by the accountant’s report 3 financial years on the Main Board; 2 on GEM Chapter 4, GEM Rule 11.11
Latest financial period relative to the listing document date Not more than 6 months Rule 4.04, GEM Rule 11.11

Note: The above are express deadlines in the rules or guidance; in practice, time must also be allowed for audit, due diligence, responding to enquiries and the market window.

Putting these checkpoints together, a reasonably smooth project roughly follows this rhythm (experience-based):

  • T-12 to T-6 months: restructuring, audit, internal control remediation and engaging intermediaries.
  • T-2 months: formal sponsor appointment (no A1 submission before this point).
  • T0: A1 submission, same-day (optional) AP publication, dual filing.
  • T+1 to T+5 months: multiple enquiry rounds and listing document revisions; where financial information is approaching the 6-month validity limit, consider a stub-period audit.
  • T+5 to T+6 months: hearing, PHIP, registration, roadshow and pricing, launch.
  • Around T+6 months: listing. Where there are many enquiry rounds or additional audit is needed, slippage to 9–12 months overall is common.

It should be emphasised that the 6-month validity of the A1 is a “countdown”, not a “target”. Once a stub-period audit or slow enquiries make completion within 6 months impossible, the project must be resubmitted with the fee paid again, significantly increasing the time cost.

7. Fee Structure

7.1 Initial Listing Fees Charged by HKEX

The Main Board initial listing fee is charged by tier according to the monetary value of the securities to be listed and must be paid in advance at the time of application (Main Board Fees Rules).

Table 10 Main Board Initial Listing Fees (Summary)

Monetary value of securities to be listed (HK$ million) Initial listing fee (HK$)
Not exceeding 100 150,000
Not exceeding 200 175,000
Not exceeding 300 200,000
Not exceeding 400 225,000
Not exceeding 500 250,000
Not exceeding 750 300,000
Not exceeding 1,000 350,000
Not exceeding 1,500 400,000
Not exceeding 2,000 450,000
Not exceeding 3,000 550,000
Not exceeding 4,000 600,000
Not exceeding 5,000 600,000
Over 5,000 650,000

Note: The brackets are progressive tiers (“not exceeding”); the HK$25 million tier corresponds to an HK$500,000 fee; the current Main Board Fees Rules prevail. A separate fee schedule applies to GEM.

7.2 Intermediary Costs

Beyond exchange fees, the main cost of an IPO comes from intermediaries. The ranges below reflect market experience and are for budgeting reference only; actual fees depend on project size, complexity, number of enquiry rounds and offering size:

Table 11 Principal Intermediary Fees (Market Reference, Not Official Data)

Item Basis of charging Order of magnitude
Sponsor fee Fixed fee, paid in stages Usually several million Hong Kong dollars, depending on size and complexity
Underwriting commission Percentage of offering size Usually around 2.5%–4.0%, including management and incentive fees
Legal advisers Hourly or capped Combined Hong Kong, PRC and offshore counsel typically in the millions
Reporting accountant Based on workload and stages In the millions, rising with consolidation scope and audit complexity
Valuation / internal control / industry consultants Quoted per project From several hundred thousand to several million Hong Kong dollars
Printing, translation, PR, roadshow Based on volume of services From several hundred thousand to several million Hong Kong dollars

Note: The above does not constitute a quotation. Total fees as a proportion of funds raised vary widely with project size and are typically lower for large projects than for small and medium-sized ones; ongoing post-listing compliance costs should also be factored in.

8. Offering and Pricing Mechanisms

8.1 Offering Structure

  • Public offer: aimed at retail investors, typically 10% of the global offering initially; over-subscription triggers the clawback mechanism, with the clawback percentage applied according to the tiered scale disclosed in the prospectus (commonly 15x, 50x and 100x tiers).
  • Placing: aimed at institutional and professional investors, coordinated by the OC through bookbuilding; the placing portion typically accounts for 90%.
  • Pool A/Pool B: the public offer portion is divided equally into two pools, with Pool A for applicants applying for HK$5 million or less and Pool B for those applying for more than HK$5 million; where one pool is under-subscribed, the surplus is transferred to the other pool (PN18).
  • Cornerstone investors: institutional investors that commit to subscribe before listing, usually subject to a 6-month lock-up; an excessively high cornerstone allocation squeezes the public offer portion and must be disclosed in the prospectus.
  • Over-allotment option (greenshoe): underwriters may over-allot up to 15% of the shares during the stabilisation period to dampen post-listing volatility.

8.2 Settlement and Clearing

FINI (Fast Interface for New Issuance) is HKEX’s IPO settlement platform, launched in November 2023, which compresses the settlement cycle from pricing to listing from T+5 to T+2, significantly reducing market and credit risk during the offering period. Issuers, sponsors, receiving banks, registrars and HKSCC all coordinate through the platform.

A longer-term change is the migration of the cash market as a whole to T+1: HKEX published its consultation conclusions in October 2026, targeting implementation in the second half of 2028, subject to market readiness and regulatory approval. The direct implication for IPO projects is that launch execution and settlement processes will be compressed again, and issuers and intermediaries need to adjust their internal processes in advance.

9. Review Focus and Common Issues

SEHK and SFC enquiries are not random; the vast majority fall into the following categories. Preparing in advance can significantly reduce the number of enquiry rounds.

9.1 Business and Suitability

  • Business substance: revenue recognition policies, customer and supplier concentration, abnormal gross margins, related-party transactions, and consistency between fund flows and contracts.
  • Sustainability: industry cycles, policy dependence, risk of losing major customers, sources of core technology and ownership of intellectual property.
  • Suitability: management integrity, historical equity defects, administrative penalties, controlling shareholder background; SEHK may reject an application on the ground of “unsuitability for listing”.

9.2 Structure and Independence

  • Competing business: where a controlling shareholder operates a competing business, disclosure must be made under Rule 8.10 of the reasons for exclusion, the scale of the competing business and evidence of independence.
  • Connected transactions: continuing connected transactions after listing must comply with Chapter 14A; unnecessary related-party dealings must be eliminated before listing.
  • VIE structure: validity of the contractual arrangements, compliance with foreign exchange and foreign investment access rules, and adequacy of risk disclosure.

9.3 Financials and Internal Controls

  • Reporting accountant’s report: three financial years on the Main Board and two on GEM; the latest financial period must not be more than 6 months before the listing document.
  • Internal controls: the degree to which processes such as treasury management, procurement and sales, inventory and approval of connected transactions are institutionalised; internal control adviser reports are often required.
  • Tax and social security: historical underpayments, reliance on tax incentives and transfer pricing on cross-border transactions.

9.4 Offering and Public Float

  • Public float and free float: the market-cap-tiered public float percentage, 300 shareholders, the 50% cap on the top three public shareholders and the free float threshold—failure on any one of these prevents listing.
  • Independence of cornerstones and the underwriting syndicate: independence of cornerstone investors, source of subscription funds and whether any side agreements exist.
  • Pre-IPO investment: fairness of the entry price, whether special rights have been terminated, and whether the investment amounts to last-minute pre-IPO shareholding.

9.5 The Most Common “Blockers”

Table 12 High-Frequency Blockers and Responses

Blocker Consequence Response
A1 documents not “substantially complete” Application returned; 8-week wait before resubmission Sponsor performs a completeness check before submission; all main sections of the listing document in place
Not completed within 6 months Application lapses, fee not refunded, resubmission required Work back from the deadline; schedule a stub-period audit before the financial information expires
Insufficient public float/free float Listing conditions cannot be met Design the offering size and secondary share sale in advance; model each tier
Competing business/connected transactions not cleaned up Repeated enquiries, hearing delays Resolve during restructuring; avoid filing a defective application
Questionable earnings quality More enquiry rounds, valuation pressure Standardise revenue recognition; prepare customer and fund-flow verification working papers

Note: The above summarises practical experience and does not represent a regulatory position.

10. Rule Changes in 2025–2026

  • New public float and free float framework (effective 4 August 2025): the flat 25% requirement was replaced by market-cap tiers (25%/15%/10%), and a free float requirement was introduced (≥10% and market cap ≥ HK$50 million, or market cap ≥ HK$600 million). This is more flexible for large issuers but places greater emphasis on genuinely tradable shares for small and medium-sized issuers.
  • Optional publication of the Application Proof: the current Rule 12.01A is framed as “if the applicant elects to publish”; where the applicant elects to publish, the AP must be submitted on the same day as the A1. Applicants that do not elect to publish must still publish a PHIP after the hearing.
  • Chapter 18C market cap and revenue thresholds: commercialised Specialist Technology companies—market cap at listing of not less than HK$6 billion and Specialist Technology revenue of not less than HK$250 million in the most recent audited year; pre-commercial companies—market cap of not less than HK$10 billion, with no revenue requirement.
  • FINI enhancements: a round of functional upgrades in 2025 further reduced manual steps in launch execution.
  • T+1 consultation conclusions (October 2026): the cash market targets T+1 implementation in the second half of 2028, subject to market readiness and regulatory approval; T+2 remains in place for now.

11. Practical Recommendations

  • Treat sponsor appointment as the T-2 starting point: because of the statutory 2-month interval, the later the sponsor is in place, the later the A1 is filed; start sponsor selection as soon as the restructuring plan has largely taken shape.
  • Fix “hard defects” before discussing valuation: competing business, connected transactions, equity defects and missing licences are structural issues; leaving them to the enquiry stage often leads to hearing delays or even withdrawal.
  • Front-load audit and internal controls: the three-year (or two-year) financial statements and internal control remediation sit on the longest critical path and should run in parallel with, not after, restructuring.
  • Plan backwards from the 6-month validity period: convert enquiry rounds, stub-period audits, hearing scheduling and the market window into weeks, and build in a buffer of at least 4–6 weeks.
  • Enquiry responses should be “complete” rather than “fast”: the rules expressly prohibit fragmented revisions; each version of the listing document should address all comments in one go, otherwise a redo may be required.
  • Design the offering structure and public float together: offering size, secondary share sales, cornerstone allocation and the clawback mechanism jointly determine whether the public float and free float thresholds are met, and should be modelled before submission.
  • Watch the market window: passing review does not guarantee a successful launch; pricing and demand depend on the window, and where necessary it is better to delay the offering than to price reluctantly.

item.title: The Way of Heaven and the Way of Man: The Ancient Wisdom Behind the Wealth Gap
item.description:
Note: This is my original note and commentary based on episode 7 of the AI Historical Anecdotes series by the Douyin account “Who Moved My History”. It is not a verbatim transcript. The original video was published on 2026-09-03, and the creator states the content is AI-generated. Original video: v.douyin.com/6XIgWJ9wKLM

The video is framed as a dialogue with Laozi and uses the Daodejing’s line “The Way of Heaven reduces the surplus to supplement the deficient; the Way of Man does the opposite, taking from the deficient to serve the surplus” as its thesis. It explains the operating rules behind the wealth gap and offers a methodology for ordinary people to break through.

I. The Core Proposition: One Sentence That Reveals the Law of the World

The Way of Heaven reduces the surplus to supplement the deficient; The Way of Man is different: it takes from the deficient to serve the surplus. — Daodejing

This sentence reveals two layers of rules:

The Way of Heaven (natural law) The Way of Man (social law)
Direction Reduce the surplus, supplement the deficient (take from the rich to help the poor; maintain balance) Take from the deficient, serve the surplus (take from the poor to enrich the rich; the strong get stronger)
Goal Seek balance; no single power may dominate Reward the strong; devour the weak
Analogy Eagles breed slowly, sparrows breed quickly; the top is capped Snowballing; the Matthew Effect

A natural person asks: Why does the Way of Heaven support the weak, while the Way of Man robs the poor to enrich the rich?

II. Why Does the Way of Heaven “Cut Peaks and Fill Valleys”? — Nature’s Invisible Hand

  • Use ecological niches as an analogy: a sparrow lays five or six eggs per clutch and has two or three clutches a year; an eagle lays only one or two eggs a year, and its chicks have a high mortality rate.
  • If eagles also bred wildly and all their chicks survived, they would eat all their prey and eventually go extinct themselves.
  • → This is “reducing the surplus to supplement the deficient”: nature firmly caps the reproductive lifeline of apex predators in order to preserve life at the bottom.
  • Conclusion: The Way of Heaven does not allow one power to dominate or a winner to take all.

III. Why Does the Way of Man Work in Reverse? — “Social Consensus” and the Matthew Effect

The Way of Man works in the opposite direction because human society has built a system of “social consensus”. The modern scholar Robert K. Merton coined the term “Matthew Effect” for the same phenomenon, and it is the core of the Way of Man:

For to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

An academic example: the same paper —

  • with a giant’s name attached → causes a sensation;
  • with an unknown author’s name attached → gathers dust in a pile of papers.
  • Fame automatically mints more fame; capital automatically breeds more capital.

A coffee shop example: two coffee shops open on the same street at the same time —

  • the one on the left hangs a well-known chain’s sign: headquarters handles site selection and the supply chain, and people come on day one because of the brand;
  • the one on the right is run by a young independent owner. The coffee is just as good, but few people walk in during the first month.

The reason: the left one has endorsement and backing, so customers do not have to take a risk; the right one may be better, but nobody knows about it.

The cruelty of the Way of Man is this: it only looks at whether you have initial chips in your hand. For the same mistake, someone with chips gets a scratch; someone without chips is out of the game. The gap widens bit by bit. In the end it looks like a gap in ability, but from the very beginning it was a gap in chips. “The system itself rewards the strong and devours the weak.”

IV. Can the Rules of the Way of Man Be Broken? — You Cannot Escape the Circle Drawn by the Way of Heaven

Man follows the earth, the earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, and the Way follows nature.

  • No matter how much the Way of Man jumps around, it cannot escape the circle drawn by the Way of Heaven.
  • When something that once flourished reaches a critical point, the balancing mechanism of the Way of Heaven kicks in: the too-strong are weakened, the too-concentrated are dispersed.
  • But the key is: that critical point will not come looking for you. You have to create the conditions yourself and make it tilt in your direction.

A Methodology for Breaking Through (Step by Step)

Step 1 | Let go of emotions

  • Many people, once they see the nature of “the rich getting richer”, become cynical. But emotion is the cheapest thing there is; it traps you in a dead end.
  • Analogy: when a strong wind hits at sea, cursing the sky will not move the boat. A real sailor shuts up immediately, watches the wind, and adjusts the sails.
  • → Acknowledge that the system exists, treat it as objective terrain, and then look for leverage.

Step 2 | First “have” a snowball, rather than “roll” one

  • The Way of Man is like snowballing: if you already have a snowball, one push makes it bigger; if you do not, the most important thing is not to find a steep slope but to first pack a ball of snow.
  • The essence of being “deficient” = not yet having an initial snowball (no resources, no endorsement).
  • → The urgent question is not “how to roll” but “how to first have something”.

Step 3 | Let people see you first

  • You have done a lot of work but nobody sees it? That is the biggest problem.
  • You must first make people notice you; only then will they come near you and give you resources.
  • Do not believe that “gold will always shine”. If you do not show it, nobody knows what you are made of. Let people see you first.

Step 4 | One word: “good” — be patient and accumulate

  • Most people do not lose at the starting line; they lose to impatience: they act blindly when provoked and lie flat when frustrated.
  • People who truly gain a foothold are those who quietly accumulate strength for a long time in a corner where nobody is watching.
  • The bamboo analogy: it can shoot up because its roots have accumulated nutrients across hundreds of square meters underground. The roots go deep.

Step 5 | The highest good is like water: work with a high profile, live with a low profile

  • After accumulating resources, you must remember another line: the highest good is like water — water nourishes all things yet always stays in the lowest place.
  • If you show your edge and sit high above others, the Way of Heaven will immediately suppress you. A good line: work with a high profile, but live with a low profile.
  • Showing is necessary, but “what to show, how much to show, and when to show” matters:

    Let others see that you are doing things, but do not let them see through what you are thinking. Put your abilities on the table; keep your thoughts in your belly.

V. For Managers: Plant Seeds of the Way of Heaven Within the Framework of the Way of Man

  • Teams also follow the Way of Man: high performers get more resources, while average performers are gradually pushed out.
  • If left alone, the team will inevitably end up with a few people holding all the opportunities while the rest coast, and efficiency will decline.
  • A good manager must plant seeds of the Way of Heaven within the framework of the Way of Man:
    • when a big tree blocks all the sunlight, as the person who sets the rules, you must cut away the excess branches;
    • bind the interests of the strong to the growth of newcomers;
    • assign people who compete for credit to different projects so they compete separately;
    • when the system is about to monopolize, you must be the “heaven” that starts “reducing the surplus to supplement the deficient”.

VI. Conclusion: Understand and Use Both the Way of Heaven and the Way of Man

The Way of Heaven gives me awe and balance; the Way of Man forces me to show and accumulate. A low starting point is not frightening. What is frightening is being kidnapped by anger and refusing to think about how to make the rules work for you. The Way of Heaven and the Way of Man are not a choice between two; you must understand and use both at the same time — the Way of Heaven gives you the bottom line and the direction; the Way of Man gives you the methods and the path.

If you want to change, the best time is to start right now.

Process Architecture (process tree)

1
2

systemd(1)
 └─ chrome(92439) ← Chrome main process
 ├─ mcp-chrome-bridge(92929, process name: MainThread)
 │ └─ listening on 127.0.0.1:12306 (HTTP)
 ├─ chrome(92508) ← renderer/GPU/network child processes
 └─ ...

Key facts

  • Who starts mcp-chrome-bridge? — Chrome does. Chrome reads the Native Messaging Host configuration (/etc/opt/chrome/native-messaging-hosts/com.chromemcp.nativehost.json) and automatically launches mcp-chrome-bridge as a child process at startup.
  • Shared or one per Claude session? — Shared. There is only one daemon. It has been running since July 19, and all Claude sessions connect to the same 127.0.0.1:12306.
  • Are Chrome and mcp-chrome-bridge independent processes? — They have a parent-child relationship. Chrome is the parent; mcp-chrome-bridge is the child.

Three-tier Interaction Architecture

│ chrome-control MCP tools │
└──────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
 │ ① HTTP (127.0.0.1:12306/mcp)
 ▼
┌─ mcp-chrome-bridge daemon ──────────────┐
│ Child process of Chrome, PID 92929 │
│ Does two things at once: │
│ • HTTP service (port 12306) │
│ • Native Messaging communication │
└──────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
 │ ② Native Messaging (stdin/stdout pipe)
 ▼
┌─ Chrome Extension ──────────────────────┐
│ Name: chrome-mcp-server │
│ Version: 1.0.0 │
│ ID: hbdgbgagpkpjffpklnamcljpakneikee │
│ Type: persistent background Service Worker │
│ chrome.runtime.connectNative() │
└──────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
 │ ③ CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol)
 ▼
┌─ Chrome browser ────────────────────────┐
│ Open tabs, page content, DOM │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Native Messaging Protocol

This is the standard mechanism for communication between a Chrome extension and a local program. It is a pipe, not a network port.

Registration

The Native Messaging Host configuration file tells Chrome how to start the local program:

/etc/opt/chrome/native-messaging-hosts/com.chromemcp.nativehost.json

1
2
3
4
5
6

{
 "name": "com.chromemcp.nativehost",
 "path": "/usr/local/.../mcp-chrome-bridge/dist/run_host.sh",
 "type": "stdio",
 "allowed_origins": [
 "chrome-extension://hbdgbgagpkpjffpklnamcljpakneikee/"
 ]
}
  • type: "stdio" — communicates over stdin/stdout
  • path — the program Chrome should launch
  • allowed_origins — only the specified extension may connect

Message format

 1
 2
 3
 4

┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ 4 bytes │ JSON data │
│ (length) │ (UTF-8 encoded JSON string)│
│ little- │ │
│ endian │ │
├──────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ 0x1A │ {"type":"request",...} │
│ 0x00 │ │
│ 0x00 │ │
│ 0x00 │ │
└──────────┴─────────────────────────────┘
  1. Write a 4-byte little-endian integer indicating the length of the JSON that follows.
  2. Write the JSON string.
  3. The receiver reads 4 bytes to get the length, then reads exactly that many bytes of JSON.

Chrome Extension API

The Chrome extension establishes a connection with chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.chromemcp.nativehost'), which returns a Port object. It communicates through port.postMessage() and port.onMessage.

Full Request Flow (using get_windows_and_tabs as an example)

Step 2: The mcp-chrome-bridge MCP Server (stdio CLI) receives the call
 ↓ HTTP POST (127.0.0.1:12306/mcp)
Step 3: The mcp-chrome-bridge daemon (port 12306) receives the request
 ↓ forwards it internally to the Native Messaging Host module
Step 4: The Native Messaging Host serializes the request to JSON
 ↓ writes it to stdout in Native Messaging format
Step 5: The Chrome extension's stdin receives the message
 ↓ parses the JSON and recognizes the get_windows_and_tabs command
Step 6: The extension queries Chrome for window/tab information via CDP
 ↓ CDP requests: Target.getTargets, Browser.getWindowForTarget, etc.
Step 7: Chrome returns the CDP response
 ↓ the extension receives the window/tab data
Step 8: The extension serializes the result to JSON
 ↓ writes it to stdout in Native Messaging format
Step 9: mcp-chrome-bridge's stdin receives the response
 ↓ parses the JSON and prepares the HTTP response
Step 10: The daemon returns HTTP 200 + JSON data
 ↓
Step 11: The MCP Server receives the response and returns it to Claude
 ↓

Simplified data flow

2

Claude ← HTTP ← mcp-chrome-bridge ← stdin/stdout ← Chrome extension ← CDP ←

Network Ports

Port Process Purpose
12306 MainThread (mcp-chrome-bridge) HTTP MCP endpoint for Claude
(none) Chrome extension Communicates over stdin/stdout, no network

Installation (other machines)

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 20+
  • npm / pnpm
  • Chrome browser

Steps

1. Install mcp-chrome-bridge globally

1

npm install -g mcp-chrome-bridge

The postinstall script runs automatically and registers the user-level Native Messaging Host.

2. Register the Native Messaging Host

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

# Auto-detect installed browsers and register
mcp-chrome-bridge register --detect

# Or specify a browser
mcp-chrome-bridge register --browser chrome

# System-level installation (all users)
sudo mcp-chrome-bridge register -s

After registration, a configuration file is created at ~/.config/google-chrome/NativeMessagingHosts/com.chromemcp.nativehost.json.

3. Install the Chrome extension

Install the chrome-mcp-server extension from the Chrome Web Store:

1

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/chrome-mcp-server/hbdgbgagpkpjffpklnamcljpakneikee

In the extension management page, confirm the extension ID is hbdgbgagpkpjffpklnamcljpakneikee and that the Service Worker is running in the background.

4. Verify the installation

1
2

# Run diagnostics
mcp-chrome-bridge doctor

Confirm that the key items are all [OK]:

1
2
3
4
5

[OK] Installation: mcp-chrome-bridge@1.0.31
[OK] Host files: run_host.sh is executable
[OK] Chrome manifest: NativeMessagingHosts/com.chromemcp.nativehost.json
[OK] Port config: http://127.0.0.1:12306/mcp
[OK] Connectivity: GET http://127.0.0.1:12306/ping -> 200

5. Configure ~/.claude.json

 1
 2
 3
 4

10

{
 "mcpServers": {
 "chrome-control": {
 "command": "node",
 "args": [
 "mcp-chrome-stdio"
 ]
 }
 }
}

mcp-chrome-bridge registers the mcp-chrome-stdio command automatically after installation. An absolute path also works:

1

/usr/local/node-v24.14.0-linux-x64/lib/node_modules/mcp-chrome-bridge/dist/mcp/mcp-server-stdio.js

Find the exact path with npm list -g mcp-chrome-bridge.

6. Restart Chrome and Claude Code

When Chrome restarts, it automatically launches the mcp-chrome-bridge child process, which listens on port 12306. After Claude Code restarts, the chrome-control tools are available.

How It Works

Layer Protocol Components
Claude → bridge HTTP (port 12306) MCP Server ↔ mcp-chrome-bridge daemon
Bridge → Chrome extension Native Messaging (stdin/stdout) Daemon ↔ Chrome Extension
Extension → page CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) The extension controls browser tabs through CDP

Key points

  • No --remote-debugging-port startup flag is required.
  • No socket/pipe files are involved.
  • Native Messaging uses a stdin/stdout pipe; the message format is [4-byte length][JSON].
  • The Chrome extension uses CDP internally to access tabs — the same protocol used by DevTools.

What It Can Do

Tab management

Tool Description
get_windows_and_tabs List all windows and tabs, including URLs and titles
chrome_switch_tab Switch to a specific tab
chrome_close_tabs Close specified tabs
chrome_navigate Navigate the current tab to a new URL, refresh the page, or go back/forward

Page reading

Tool Description
chrome_read_page Read the page’s accessibility tree to get the page structure and visible elements. Can filter to interactive elements only (buttons/links/inputs) and can extract plain text
chrome_get_web_content Get visible text or HTML content, with CSS selector support for specific regions
chrome_screenshot Capture a screenshot of the current page or a specific element

Page interaction

Tool Description
chrome_click_element Click an element (CSS selector, XPath, element ref, or viewport coordinates). Supports left/right/middle button, double-click, and modifier keys (Ctrl/Shift/Alt)
chrome_fill_or_select Fill forms (inputs, textareas, selects, checkboxes, radio buttons)
chrome_keyboard Simulate keyboard input (single keys, shortcuts like Ctrl+C, text input), optionally targeting a specific element
chrome_computer Combined operations: mouse click/drag/scroll, keyboard input, wait, zoom, screenshot
chrome_upload_file Upload files through a file picker (local path, URL download, or base64 data)
chrome_handle_dialog Handle JavaScript dialogs (alert/confirm/prompt) by accepting or dismissing

JavaScript execution

Tool Description
chrome_javascript Execute arbitrary JavaScript in the page context, with top-level await support and a return value

Forms and network

Tool Description
chrome_network_capture Start/stop capturing network requests, including request/response details and optional response bodies
chrome_console Capture page console output (log/warn/error) in Buffer or snapshot mode
chrome_network_request Send network requests directly from the browser with the browser’s cookies and context

GIF recording

Tool Description
chrome_gif_recorder Record a tab interaction as an animated GIF. Supports fixed-FPS mode and auto-capture mode (captures a frame after each action), with configurable FPS, duration, size, click indicators, and action labels

Performance analysis

Tool Description
performance_start_trace Start a performance trace, with optional page reload and auto-stop duration
performance_stop_trace Stop the trace and export the Trace JSON
performance_analyze_insight Analyze the recorded trace and produce performance insights

Browser management

Tool Description
chrome_bookmark_search Search bookmarks
chrome_bookmark_add Add a bookmark
chrome_bookmark_delete Delete a bookmark
chrome_history Search browsing history
chrome_handle_download Wait for and get download details

What It Cannot Do

  • Access pages that are not open
  • Read browsing history, bookmarks, or passwords
  • Install extensions or change browser settings
  • Access the content of closed tabs

Limitations

JavaScript cannot run when CDP is occupied

The chrome-mcp-server extension itself holds the CDP connection. When CDP is occupied, chrome_javascript falls back to chrome.scripting.executeScript (isolated world), but in practice the fallback also fails to return results. This means that in some scenarios you cannot extract data in bulk through JavaScript.

No structured data extraction tools

Missing capability Impact
Built-in DOM query / CSS selector data extraction List pages (such as torrent lists) only yield plain text, requiring an external Python script for a second parsing pass
No page.$$eval() equivalent There is no Playwright/Puppeteer-style way to run a selector on the page and return structured JSON
Unstructured return values chrome_get_web_content and chrome_read_page both return plain text, so tabular data loses its row/column structure

Scenario comparison

Scenario chrome-control Playwright/Puppeteer
Clicking, filling forms, navigation ✅ Convenient ✅ Convenient
Reading visible page text ✅ Works ✅ Works
Bulk list extraction ❌ Needs external parsing ✅ One line with page.$$eval()
Operating on already-logged-in pages ✅ Native support ❌ You handle cookies yourself
Screenshots ✅ ✅

Workarounds

If you need bulk data extraction, consider a dedicated browser automation MCP:

1

claude mcp add playwright -- npx -y @playwright/mcp

Or use a Python + Playwright script and bypass the MCP layer entirely.

Session Reuse

Login state (cookies/session) in Chrome is inherited automatically. For a site already logged in in a tab (such as M-Team), operating in that tab’s context carries the login state.

FAQ

The Chrome Control MCP server is not connected

1

The Chrome control MCP server is currently not connected

Possible causes:

  • The configuration in ~/.claude.json was modified or deleted
  • The mcp-chrome-bridge daemon is not running (nothing is listening on port 12306)
  • The Chrome extension is disabled or uninstalled
  • The mcp-chrome-bridge child process did not start correctly after Chrome restarted

Resolution:

  1. Confirm the chrome-control configuration exists in ~/.claude.json
  2. Check whether port 12306 is listening: ss -tlnp | grep 12306
  3. Check whether the Chrome extension hbdgbgagpkpjffpklnamcljpakneikee is enabled
  4. Restart Chrome (this also restarts the mcp-chrome-bridge child process)
  5. Restart Claude Code

Tool calls fail with “Failed to connect to MCP server” / “Already connected to a transport”

Symptoms: All chrome-control tool calls fail with Failed to connect to MCP server, while claude mcp list still shows ✔ Connected.

Root cause (diagnosed on 2026-08-12): In mcp-chrome-bridge 1.0.31, the daemon (dist/server/index.js) uses a singleton MCP Server (getMcpServer() in dist/mcp/mcp-server.js) to connect every new transport in the /mcp and /sse routes. The MCP SDK’s Protocol.connect() allows only one transport (protocol.js throws “Already connected to a transport”). Once a client disconnects abnormally and the transport does not fire onclose, the singleton is stuck forever, and all subsequent connections are rejected. The daemon’s stderr log fills with ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT (the old log grew beyond 200 MB).

Fix (patched in dist/):

  1. dist/mcp/mcp-server.js: add a createMcpServer() factory that returns an independent Server instance with tools registered each time
  2. dist/server/index.js: change the /mcp and /sse routes to use createMcpServer() (instead of getMcpServer()), giving each connection its own Server
  3. dist/server/index.js GET /mcp route: remove the manual SSE header pre-write (setHeader/flushHeaders) and hand header writing entirely to the SDK transport after reply.hijack(), eliminating ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT

Verification: single end-to-end connection ✓, 3 concurrent clients all connected ✓, zero errors in the log ✓.

Note: The patch modifies the compiled dist/ output directly, so upgrading the npm package overwrites it. Re-apply the patch after upgrading. The backup made during the fix has been deleted; back up with cp before changing anything.

Recovery steps:

  1. Kill the broken daemon (the Chrome extension will automatically reconnect and start a new one): 
    1
2

    ss -tlnp | grep 12306 # find the pid
kill <pid>
  2. If a session still cannot connect (its stdio client cached the old connection), restart that Claude session or reconnect via /mcp.

Chrome does not respond to operations

If an operation hangs and never returns, possible causes:

  • A dialog is open on the page (alert/confirm/prompt)
  • The page is still loading
  • An unclosed modal is present

Resolution: use chrome_handle_dialog to handle dialogs, or close them manually and retry.

Element not found

If chrome_read_page does not return the target element:

  • The element is outside the viewport; scroll to it with scroll_to and retry
  • The element is inside an iframe; specify frameId

item.title: Mounting an External ext4 Disk on Windows (WSL2)
item.description:
Mounting an external ext4 disk through WSL2 on Windows, and mapping the mount point to a Windows drive letter, gives you native Linux read/write access plus access from Windows Explorer. Here is the complete workflow.

Preparation (after each time you connect the disk)

1. Find the external disk number

Open PowerShell as Administrator and run the following command to identify the disk number:

1

Get-CimInstance -Query "SELECT * from Win32_DiskDrive"

In the returned list, find the model of your portable disk (for example, Innostor Ext. HDD USB Device) and look at the number at the end of the corresponding DeviceID (for example, \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE2 means disk number 2).

2. Take the disk offline in Windows

In an Administrator PowerShell:

1
2
3
4

diskpart
select disk 2
offline disk
exit

Note: if the disk number is not 2, replace the number in select disk 2 with the actual number found in step 1.

3. Attach the raw disk to the WSL2 kernel

In an Administrator PowerShell:

1

wsl --mount \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE2 --bare

Mount the filesystem and configure permissions (Linux side)

4. Find the ext4 partition and mount it

Enter Linux with wsl, run lsblk -f to confirm the partition whose TYPE is ext4 (assume it is sdd3), then run:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

# Create the mount point (only needed once)
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/ext4_usb

# Mount the ext4 partition
sudo mount /dev/sdd3 /mnt/ext4_usb

# Give Windows full read/write access
sudo chmod -R 777 /mnt/ext4_usb

Map to a Windows drive letter

5. Map drive Z: (must use a normal user)

Press Win + R, type powershell, and press Enter (do not run as Administrator), then run:

1

subst Z: \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\mnt\ext4_usb

After that, you can double-click Z: in This PC and read/write it directly.

Safely remove/eject the disk

1. Remove the drive letter (normal user terminal)

1

subst Z: /D

2. Unmount the mount point in Linux (run inside wsl)

1

sudo umount /mnt/ext4_usb

3. Detach the disk from WSL in Windows (Administrator PowerShell)

1

wsl --unmount \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE2

4. Make Windows recognize the disk again (Administrator PowerShell)

1
2
3
4

diskpart
select disk 2
online disk
exit

item.title: K8s API Auth and Grant
item.description:
I wanted to access and control the Kubernetes API using certificates. I looked around online but did not find a single good write-up, so I collected a few articles and put them together. It is a bit messy, but the general idea is clear. Feel free to take what is useful.

API Server

kube-apiserver is one of the most important core components of Kubernetes. Its main responsibilities are:

  • Providing the REST API for cluster management, including authentication, authorization, data validation, and cluster state changes
  • Acting as the hub for data exchange and communication between other modules (other modules query or modify data through the API Server; only the API Server directly operates on etcd)

REST API

kube-apiserver can serve both HTTPS (listening on port 6443 by default) and HTTP (listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 by default). The HTTP API is insecure and performs no authentication or authorization; do not enable it in production. Both endpoints expose the same REST API format. See the Kubernetes API Reference for the call format of every API.

Local port

  • Receives HTTP requests
  • Defaults to 8080; change it with the API Server’s --insecure-port startup flag
  • Defaults to the localhost IP; change it with the --insecure-bind-address startup flag
  • Unauthenticated and unauthorized HTTP requests reach the API Server through this port

Secure port

  • Defaults to 6443; change it with the --secure-port startup flag
  • The default IP is a non-local host network address; set it with the --bind-address startup flag
  • Receives HTTPS requests
  • Used for authentication based on token files, client certificates, and HTTP Basic auth
  • Used for policy-based authorization
  • HTTPS access control is not enabled by default

For a typical application, the user provides a username and password, the server checks the database to see whether they exist and are valid, and authentication succeeds or fails accordingly.

How does Kubernetes do it?

Although ordinary users cannot be created through API calls, Kubernetes cleverly authenticates users via certificates. In other words, any user who can present a valid certificate is authenticated by Kubernetes.

After authentication, Kubernetes treats the certificate’s CN as the username (for example, /CN=joker means the username is Joker) and the Organization as the user’s group. A Role bound to that username and group then determines the user’s permissions.

item.title: AWS DynamoDB Basic Usage
item.description:
DynamoDB Basic Concepts

Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service that provides fast, predictable performance and seamless scalability.

Basic structure

DynamoDB has a few core concepts: tables, items, and attributes. A table is a collection of items, and each item is a collection of attributes. You can think of them as the equivalent of collections, documents, and fields in MongoDB.

Primary keys in DynamoDB

Unlike MongoDB, DynamoDB does not generate an _id by default to uniquely identify a record. That is why DynamoDB has the concept of a primary key. You specify the primary key of a table, and the primary key uniquely identifies each item in the table (by designating one attribute as the primary key).

DynamoDB supports two kinds of primary keys:

  • 1. Partition key DynamoDB uses the value of the partition key as the input to an internal hash function. The output of the hash function determines the partition where the item is stored (the physical storage inside DynamoDB).
  • 2. Composite primary key (partition key and sort key) DynamoDB uses the partition key value as the input to an internal hash function. The output of the hash function determines the partition where the item is stored (the physical storage inside DynamoDB). All items with the same partition key are stored together, sorted by the sort key value.

In a table with a partition key and a sort key, two items may have the same partition key value, but they must have different sort key values.

  1. Download and extract DynamoDB Local
